network.overall_strategy: Threonine is treated as a late, low-flux product that should accumulate only in cool surface or prebiotic-pool settings. The network therefore uses the two best-supported threonine chemistries from the literature: a cyanosulfidic surface sequence that upgrades formaldehyde and HCN to lactaldehyde and then to a nonselective threonine aminonitrile pool, and a separate Cu-assisted aldol capture of independently available glycine by acetaldehyde. Ten pathways are represented as distinct precursor-entry routes through these two connected modules; allothreonine is kept explicit, while productive hydrothermal threonine synthesis is omitted because current evidence for it is poor and threonine is thermally fragile at high temperature.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation of glycolonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic cyanide-rich evaporitic pool or shoreline film; near-neutral to mildly alkaline.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to formaldehyde to form the cyanohydrin glycolonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Glycolonitrile is the canonical HCN-formaldehyde adduct and a key entry point in cyanosulfidic prebiotic chemistry, linking simple C1 feedstocks to higher-carbon aldehydes and amino-acid precursors (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Patel et al., 2015). Making this node explicit avoids the overcompressed and unbalanced C1-to-C2 shortcuts criticized in earlier drafts.

reactions.name: CuCN-sulfide photoredox reduction of glycolonitrile to glycolaldehyde

conditions.other: UV-irradiated sulfidic surface pool, roughly pH 7 with phosphate buffering; elemental sulfur is written as the net oxidized sulfur product.

reactions.mechanism: Cu-mediated sulfide photoredox converts the nitrile-bearing precursor to the aldehyde, with hydrolytic loss of ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson & Sutherland demonstrated CuCN/H2S/UV reduction of cyanohydrin and nitrile pools toward carbonyl compounds, and Patel et al. embedded this logic in a wider cyanosulfidic network. Writing elemental sulfur explicitly keeps the redox bookkeeping balanced; real sulfur speciation may be more complex. Sulfidic anion availability is itself a known environmental limitation for this chemistry (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Patel et al., 2015; Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Net sulfide photoreduction of glycolaldehyde to acetaldehyde

conditions.other: UV-irradiated sulfidic pool; net sulfur oxidation is written as S(0); low-oxygen, phosphate-bearing surface setting.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide-driven photoredox reduction/deoxygenation of the C2 hydroxyaldehyde yields acetaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. derive acetaldehyde from glycolaldehyde reduction within the cyanosulfidic system. This exact isolated step is less directly quantified than the lactonitrile-to-lactaldehyde conversion, so it should be treated as network-supported rather than individually high-confidence. It is nevertheless essential because both the Strecker and aldol routes to threonine depend on acetaldehyde supply (Patel et al., 2015; Ritson & Sutherland, 2013).

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation of lactonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic cyanide-rich pool; near-neutral to mildly alkaline.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to acetaldehyde to form the cyanohydrin lactonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Acetaldehyde cyanohydrin, lactonitrile, is the direct precursor that Ritson & Sutherland photoreduced to lactaldehyde. This is therefore the chemically required link between the acetaldehyde hub and threonine's Strecker aldehyde; Cobb & Pudritz also identify lactaldehyde as the threonine Strecker aldehyde in parent-body modeling (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Cobb & Pudritz, 2015).

reactions.name: CuCN-sulfide photoredox reduction of lactonitrile to lactaldehyde

conditions.other: UV-irradiated sulfidic surface pool, roughly pH 7 with phosphate buffer; elemental sulfur is the net oxidized sulfur product.

reactions.mechanism: Cu-sulfide photoredox converts lactonitrile to lactaldehyde with hydrolytic release of ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: This is the strongest dedicated precursor step for threonine: Ritson & Sutherland reported lactaldehyde in 19% yield from lactonitrile under Cu(I)/H2S/UV conditions, explicitly identifying it as the Strecker precursor of (allo-)threonine. The balanced sulfur bookkeeping is made explicit here to avoid the mass-balance failures of earlier versions (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Strecker formation of a threonine aminonitrile pool

conditions.other: Concentrated HCN/NH3 pool; near-neutral to mildly alkaline; non-stereoselective aminonitrile formation.

reactions.mechanism: Lactaldehyde condenses with ammonia to an imine/iminium that is trapped by cyanide, yielding 2-amino-3-hydroxybutanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson & Sutherland state that added HCN and NH3 convert lactaldehyde smoothly to the (allo)threonine aminonitrile, and Patel et al. likewise describe threonine aminonitrile as an inevitable by-product of cyanosulfidic chemistry. Because the aminonitrile yield and threo:allo ratio were not reported, the node is represented as a stereochemically unresolved aminonitrile pool (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of threonine aminonitrile to threonine

conditions.other: Cool prebiotic pool or geothermal cycling; effective stoichiometry is aminonitrile + 2 H2O -> threonine + NH3.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration and hydrolysis converts the aminonitrile into the free amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: This hydrolysis is chemically required but experimentally unresolved for threonine in the cited cyanosulfidic literature, which stops at the aminonitrile stage; it is therefore partly speculative. It is placed in cool prebiotic pools because high-temperature residence rapidly destroys threonine, making hydrothermal accumulation implausible (Patel et al., 2015; Aubrey et al., 2009; Higgs & Pudritz, 2009).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of threonine aminonitrile to allothreonine

conditions.other: Cool prebiotic pool or geothermal cycling; effective stoichiometry is aminonitrile + 2 H2O -> allothreonine + NH3.

reactions.mechanism: The same nitrile-hydrolysis sequence yields the allo diastereomer from the nonselective aminonitrile pool.
reactions.reasoning: Nonenzymatic threonine chemistry is expected to be diastereomerically mixed. Trace spark residues showed roughly equal threonine and allothreonine, so an allothreonine hydrolysis branch should accompany any unresolved aminonitrile pool; keeping it explicit is more faithful to the literature than forcing a single threonine product (Ring et al., 1972 as compiled by Weber & Miller, 1981; Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Cu-assisted glycine-acetaldehyde aldol addition to threonine

conditions.other: Concentrated mildly basic pool or mineral interface, often carbonate/bicarbonate buffered; Cu-glycinate activation; reversible retro-aldol chemistry remains a sink.

reactions.mechanism: Cu-bound glycine acts as an enolate equivalent and adds to acetaldehyde, giving the beta-hydroxy alpha-amino acid after proton transfer.
reactions.reasoning: This is the only intentionally designed route that has actually produced free threonine itself rather than merely a precursor. Sato, Okawa and Akabori obtained threonine plus allothreonine from copper glycinate, and later work confirmed the strong sensitivity of yield and diastereomer ratio to catalyst and base. The route is chemically strong but geochemically weak because it relies on concentrated Cu(II) chemistry and is reversible (Sato et al., 1957; Ikutani et al., 1959).

reactions.name: Cu-assisted glycine-acetaldehyde aldol addition to allothreonine

conditions.other: Concentrated mildly basic pool or mineral interface, often carbonate/bicarbonate buffered; Cu-glycinate activation; product ratio depends strongly on base and residence time.

reactions.mechanism: The same Cu-assisted aldol addition yields the allo diastereomer when the new stereocenters form with the alternative relative configuration.
reactions.reasoning: Akabori-type chemistry is inherently diastereomeric. The literature reports both threonine and allothreonine, with threo:allo varying widely with catalyst loading, base strength and time. Explicitly including the allothreonine branch is therefore necessary for a faithful threonine network rather than an artificially selective one (Sato et al., 1957; Ikutani et al., 1959; Weber & Miller, 1981).

pathways.name: Full cyanosulfidic Strecker sequence from formaldehyde
pathways.description: Formaldehyde is trapped as glycolonitrile, reduced through glycolaldehyde and acetaldehyde to lactonitrile and lactaldehyde, then converted through a nonselective aminonitrile pool to threonine.

pathways.name: Glycolonitrile-entry Strecker route
pathways.description: Entry variant that assumes glycolonitrile is supplied by other HCN chemistry before the same surface sequence to threonine.

pathways.name: Glycolaldehyde-entry Strecker route
pathways.description: Entry at the C2 sugar stage; only acetaldehyde generation, lactonitrile/lactaldehyde formation and Strecker-hydrolysis remain.

pathways.name: Acetaldehyde-entry Strecker route
pathways.description: Entry variant in which acetaldehyde is already available from independent surface photochemistry or discharge chemistry.

pathways.name: Lactonitrile-entry Strecker route
pathways.description: Shortest dedicated precursor sequence that begins at the acetaldehyde cyanohydrin and exploits the experimentally supported photoreduction to lactaldehyde.

pathways.name: Lactaldehyde-entry Strecker route
pathways.description: Most compressed dedicated route; assumes the Strecker aldehyde for threonine is already present in a cool cyanide-ammonia pool.

pathways.name: Full Akabori-type aldol route from formaldehyde plus glycine
pathways.description: Formaldehyde is upgraded through the cyanosulfidic branch to acetaldehyde, which is then captured by independently supplied glycine in a Cu-assisted aldol reaction.

pathways.name: Glycolonitrile-entry aldol route
pathways.description: Entry variant in which glycolonitrile and glycine are already available; only acetaldehyde generation and the final aldol capture remain.

pathways.name: Glycolaldehyde-entry aldol route
pathways.description: Entry at glycolaldehyde with glycine supplied independently; this isolates acetaldehyde production as the last upstream bottleneck before aldol capture.

pathways.name: Minimal glycine-acetaldehyde aldol route
pathways.description: Direct Cu-assisted condensation of pre-existing glycine and acetaldehyde in a concentrated mildly basic prebiotic pool.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Coherent full cyanosulfidic-to-Strecker route and well aligned with the literature up to the aminonitrile. The weak point is rxn_007: hydrolysis of the threonine aminonitrile pool to free threonine is not demonstrated under clearly prebiotic conditions, its written stoichiometry should be mol_013 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_014 + mol_002, and the move from Surface to a vague Biochemical setting is not physically justified.
suggestions: Specify CuCN, phosphate, UV wavelength, and pH for rxn_002-rxn_005.
Rewrite rxn_007 with 2 H2O and cite a concrete prebiotic hydrolysis regime.
If hydrolysis remains unsupported, end the prebiotic branch at mol_013 and treat free threonine as conditional.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This shorter glycolonitrile-entry route preserves the best-supported surface photoredox chemistry and the canonical lactaldehyde Strecker step. Confidence is still capped by the Cu/H2S/UV requirements in rxn_002-rxn_005 and by rxn_007, which remains an under-supported hydrolysis-to-target step and should be written with 2 H2O.
suggestions: Make the Cu catalyst and surface photochemistry conditions explicit in rxn_002-rxn_005.
Justify transfer into a cool aqueous pool or similar setting before hydrolysis.
Rewrite rxn_007 as mol_013 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_014 + mol_002.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Starting at glycolaldehyde removes one yield-loss step but the chemistry is still dominated by photoreduction to acetaldehyde and lactaldehyde followed by Strecker capture. As in the literature, the route is convincing to the aminonitrile and much less convincing from mol_013 to free threonine via rxn_007.
suggestions: Document Cu/H2S/UV conditions and expected yields for rxn_003 and rxn_005.
Rewrite rxn_007 with the missing second water molecule.
If the network claims free threonine, add literature support for aminonitrile hydrolysis under geochemically plausible conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Acetaldehyde-entry Strecker chemistry is pathway-coherent and literature-consistent because acetaldehyde is the known branchpoint. The remaining liabilities are the modestly evidenced lactonitrile photoreduction in rxn_005 and the poorly specified hydrolysis in rxn_007, which is the decisive target-forming step.
suggestions: Annotate rxn_005 with the reported conditions and yield for lactaldehyde formation.
Rewrite rxn_007 as mol_013 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_014 + mol_002.
Provide a concrete environmental rationale for moving from the surface module into the hydrolysis setting.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest cyanosulfidic subpath because rxn_005 has direct literature precedent for lactaldehyde formation and rxn_006 is the expected Strecker capture. It still does not fully solve the hardest problem: rxn_007 has no strong prebiotic experimental support as written for free threonine release, even though the chemistry is net-balanceable.
suggestions: Keep the cited 19% lactaldehyde yield and full photoredox conditions attached to rxn_005.
Rewrite rxn_007 with 2 H2O and provide a cited hydrolysis regime.
If hydrolysis evidence is unavailable, leave this branch ending at mol_013.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: As a late-entry route from lactaldehyde, this is the cleanest and most literature-aligned Strecker subpath in the network. The route is still not approvable because rxn_007 is both environmentally vague and only balanceable with an extra water molecule in the written form, so the target step is inferred rather than demonstrated under prebiotic conditions.
suggestions: Rewrite rxn_007 as mol_013 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_014 + mol_002.
Replace Biochemical with a concrete pond, pool, or other geochemical hydrolysis environment and cite conditions.
If stereochemical detail matters, split mol_013 into separate threo and allo aminonitrile nodes.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Connected full feedstock-to-aldol route, and it correctly uses the surface module to access acetaldehyde before threonine formation. However rxn_009 compresses a Cu(II)-glycinate, base-dependent, reversible Akabori reaction into a simple Biochemical step, so the geochemical setting and product accumulation logic are under-specified.
suggestions: Specify Cu(II)-glycinate complexation, base, temperature, and pH for rxn_009.
Justify how surface-generated acetaldehyde is concentrated and transferred into the aldol environment.
Add competing sinks such as retro-aldol cleavage and acetaldehyde self-condensation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This shorter aldol route is reasonable once glycolonitrile is available and acetaldehyde can be supplied from the surface module. The bottleneck is again rxn_009, which is genuine chemistry but not yet a convincingly prebiotic one-step conversion under the stated environment.
suggestions: Make Cu(II), base, and pH explicit for rxn_009.
Explain the physical transfer or concentration step between surface photochemistry and the aldol setting.
Note retro-aldol reversibility and the expected allothreonine coproduct.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Glycolaldehyde-entry aldol chemistry is concise and reaches the target directly once acetaldehyde is formed. Still, rxn_009 needs explicit Cu complexation, base, and concentration control, and the pathway should acknowledge that the threonine-forming direction is thermodynamically and kinetically reversible.
suggestions: State the full Cu-assisted aldol conditions instead of leaving rxn_009 as a generic Biochemical step.
Discuss retro-aldol cleavage and acetaldehyde volatility as major losses.
Justify a realistic cool-pool setting for target accumulation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Shortest complete route to free threonine and aligned with classical Akabori chemistry, with the expected allothreonine side branch present elsewhere in the network. Prebiotic realism is the weakest here: rxn_009 needs explicit Cu(II)-glycinate and base conditions plus a concrete cool-pool setting rather than a generic Biochemical label.
suggestions: Specify Cu(II)-glycinate complexation, base, temperature, and pH for rxn_009.
Replace Biochemical with a concrete geochemical environment or explicitly mark this as non-prebiotic model chemistry.
Note retro-aldol reversibility and acetaldehyde self-condensation as competing sinks.

evaluation.network_feedback: Network validity is strong: the graph is connected, molecule IDs are used consistently, and the RDKit balance check reports no unbalanceable reactions. The main stoichiometric cleanup is that rxn_007 and rxn_008 should be written as mol_013 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_014 or mol_015 + mol_002. Literature alignment is also strong: the network focuses on the two best-supported threonine chemistries, keeps allothreonine explicit at the amino-acid level, and avoids unsupported hydrothermal or reductive-amination claims. The main reason confidence stays below approval is that the cyanosulfidic branch is well supported only to the aminonitrile pool, not to free threonine, while the aldol branch reaches free threonine mainly under Cu-complex, base-rich conditions that are chemically real but not yet well grounded geochemically. Replace Biochemical with a concrete cool-pool environment, make Cu, phosphate, UV, and pH explicit where relevant, justify transfer from surface photochemistry into hydrolysis or aldol settings, and consider adding retro-aldol or degradation sinks to match the literature on threonine fragility.
